key_concept: Pteridophytes are divided into four classes, Psilopsida, Lycopsida, Sphenopsida and Pteropsida, and Sphenopsida is one of them.
steps: Recall the NCERT classification of pteridophytes into four classes: Psilopsida (e.g., Psilotum), Lycopsida (e.g., Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (e.g., Equisetum) and Pteropsida (e.g., Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum).
Sphenopsida is represented by Equisetum (horsetail). It has jointed stems with whorled scale leaves, true vascular tissue, and a sporophyte as the dominant phase.
Bryophytes are divided into liverworts and mosses. They have no class Sphenopsida.
Gymnosperms and angiosperms are seed plants. Equisetum produces spores and no seeds, so Sphenopsida cannot belong to either group.
Therefore Sphenopsida belongs to the pteridophytes, which matches the official key.
why_not_others: Bryophytes have only liverworts and mosses and lack vascular tissue. Gymnosperms and angiosperms are seed-bearing plants, whereas Sphenopsida (Equisetum) reproduces by spores.
common_trap: Students sometimes confuse the 'Spheno-' prefix with Sphagnum, a moss, and wrongly pick bryophytes.
time_saving_tip: Memorise the four pteridophyte classes as 'Psi-Lyco-Spheno-Ptero', each with its example genus (Psilotum, Selaginella, Equisetum, Dryopteris).
